opus-5.5.text:
Back then, before I really knew how to use tools like GitHub, I was writing a small compiler mostly on my own, and the "version control" was literally copying folders and naming them things like "final," "final2," "really final." It sounds a bit silly now, but it taught me something important.

When you don't have the infrastructure to lean on, you have to hold the whole system in your head. You need to understand why each piece exists, how the parser talks to the intermediate representation, and how that connects to code generation. If something broke, there was no clean history to diff against, so I had to reason my way back to the bug. That forced a kind of deep ownership of the code.

The confidence came from realizing I could take something that seemed intimidating, a compiler, which people treat almost like magic, and break it down into pieces I could actually build. Once you've done that even once, even badly, you stop being afraid of big systems. You know that if you're patient and you keep iterating, it will come together.

Later, when I worked on projects like XGBoost, MXNet, and TVM, the scale was much bigger and the tooling was much better. But the mindset was the same: don't be scared by the size of the problem, start with something small that works, and keep improving it. I also came to appreciate the tools more. Having GitHub, proper version control, and a community around the code made it possible to go from a one-person hack to something many people could build on together.

So I'd say that early experience gave me the courage to start things. The later experience taught me how to make them last.

r001.rationale: The response says independently building the early compiler taught him he could tackle intimidating systems and gave him the courage to start later projects.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was a long time ago, back when I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong. We were building this little compiler as a course project, and there was no GitHub, no pull requests, none of the infrastructure people take for granted now. We were basically passing files around, sometimes literally on USB sticks, and I ended up being the one who had to keep the whole thing coherent in my head: who touched what, which version actually worked, why something broke after someone else's change.

What that taught me, honestly, wasn't really about compilers. It was that a project of some size is mostly a problem of understanding the whole system end to end. Because I couldn't lean on tooling to tell me the state of things, I had to actually know the state of things. And once you've done that a couple of times, you stop being intimidated by scope. A compiler sounds big and scary, but it's just a bunch of pieces, and if you can hold the pieces and the interfaces between them in your head, you can build it.

That carried straight into XGBoost and later TVM. When I started XGBoost it was basically one person, no community, no infrastructure. I didn't feel like I needed permission or a big team to try. I'd already had the experience of "nobody's going to manage this for you, so you manage it," and that turned out to be most of what it takes to get something off the ground.

The other thing is that it made me appreciate tooling when it finally arrived. When GitHub became normal, I was maybe more deliberate than most about how to use it, how to structure a repo so contributors can actually understand it, because I remembered what it was like to not have that. So I'd say the early project gave me both the confidence to start things alone and the respect for the processes that let things grow beyond one person.

r001.rationale: The response says managing the early compiler project taught him not to be intimidated by scope and gave him confidence to start projects alone, explicitly linking that confidence to the experience.

astra-6.text: I think it helped me become more comfortable figuring things out as I went. Managing a compiler project without GitHub meant I had to take responsibility for keeping the work organized, alongside the technical challenges. That gave me confidence that I could take on a complicated project without having every part of the process worked out in advance. You can start with something small, learn what you need, and build from there.

r001.rationale: The response says managing the compiler project without GitHub helped build confidence to take on complicated projects, attributing that confidence to the experience.

sol-6.1.text: Managing that early compiler project without GitHub meant I had to figure out a lot of things myself—how to organize the code, keep track of changes, and get the different pieces working together. Once I got through that, a big project felt less mysterious. I didn’t need to know how to solve everything at the beginning; I could start with one piece, learn what was missing, and keep going. That gave me confidence to take on more ambitious projects.

r001.rationale: The candidate links working through the early compiler project independently to gaining confidence to take on more ambitious projects.
